newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Uighurs in Kazakhstan stage protest against China. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Uighurs in Kazakhstan stage protest against China. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT]

text.p: Ethnic Uighurs staged a noisy protest outside the Chinese embassy in Kazakhstan on Thursday against what they said was Beijing's intention to execute Uighur students arrested over last month's riots in Xinjiang province.
The group of about 35 young Uighurs shouted "East Turkestan!", the Moslem Uighurs' name for China's troubled northwest province, and "Allahu akbar!" (God is great).
Chinese diplomats filmed the protesters with video recorders.

Officials in Xinjiang said on Thursday they had indicted six people in connection with anti-Chinese rioting in the province but denied allegations made by exiled Uighur separatists that China would execute two rioters.
The United National Revolutionary Front of East Turkestan, a Uighur exile group, said on Wednesday it had received information about the executions from "secret sources".

Information from the remote, closed region of mountain and desert is difficult to verify. Uighur exiles say telephone lines to Xinjiang have been cut and news often arrives days late via traders crossing the China-Kazakh border.
The group named the two Uighurs as Abu Khair and Abdu Medchit, both around 25 years old. The group said they would probably face a firing squad in Urumqi, regional capital of Xinjiang.
The Front is one of several Uighur organisations fighting for an independent East Turkestan in Xinjiang, home to a majority of Turkic-speaking Moslems like the ethnic Uighurs.
"Today we have to stop the shooting of our people," Mukhiddin Mukhlisi, spokesman for the Front, told the demonstrators in front of the Chinese embassy.
Last month's disturbances in Yining, near the border with Kazakhstan, were some of the most violent in the province since the 1949 communist takeover.

Exile groups said last month the Yining riots were sparked by the execution of about 30 Uighurs by the Chinese authorities. Chinese sources said nine people were killed and 198 wounded (Corrects from "about ten killed and 100 wounded") in the resulting disturbances.
"These executions could provoke more bloodshed in the province," Mukhlisi warned on Wednesday.

Last year, the Xinjiang authorities cracked down on Uighur secessionists after a series of violent clashes, bombings and assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
